title: Design a distributed message queue.
description: Durable log vs queue semantics: partitioning, consumer groups, delivery guarantees, backpressure, and exactly-once illusions.

data.text: **Question:** Design a distributed message queue like Kafka or SQS.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Producers publish; consumers subscribe — decoupled in time and scale
Durable: messages survive broker restarts and producer crashes
At-least-once delivery; per-partition ordering guarantee
Consumer groups: parallel consumption with offset tracking
Retention: replay from a point in time (hours/days)
Backpressure: slow consumers must not take down producers

data.caption: Partitioned log brokers with replication and consumer-group offset tracking

graph TD

    A -->|append| C[Leader - Topic/Partition 1]
    B --> D[Follower Replica]
    C --> E[Follower Replica]

    G -->|fetch by offset| C

data.text: Two classic shapes: a **distributed log** (Kafka: ordered, replayable, partitioned; consumers read by offset) and a **smart broker** (SQS/Rabbit: broker tracks queues, deletes on ack). The log design wins for stream processing, replay, and many independent consumer groups; the queue design wins for simple task distribution where nobody needs history.

items: Partitioning is the parallelism unit: key by entity id for per-entity ordering (order events for one user land on one partition); partitions >> consumers is the healthy state
Ordering scope = one partition, not the topic — say this out loud in any design review
Durability: append to leader's log, replicate to followers (ISR - in-sync replicas), ack producer after min-ISR — fsync policy trades latency for loss window
Consumer groups: coordinator assigns partitions (rebalance on membership change); offsets committed periodically — crash between process and commit ⇒ redelivery ⇒ consumers must be idempotent
Delivery guarantees: at-least-once is the honest default; 'exactly-once' inside the broker (transactions/producer idempotence) still requires idempotent side effects end-to-end
Retention: time- or size-based per topic; offsets enable replay (buggy consumer fix = reset offset and reprocess)
Backpressure: slow consumer lags; alerts on consumer lag (the health metric of a queue system); slow-lane/DLQ for poison messages so one bad message doesn't block a partition forever
Fetch model: long-polling batch fetches (batch.size, linger) turn chatty RPCs into throughput; latency-sensitive topics use small batches
Metadata/coordination: partition leaders, group coordinators, and membership via etcd/ZooRaft-style store; leader failover promotes a caught-up follower
Priority/delayed queues: log designs fake these poorly (separate topics); SQS-style brokers model them natively — pick per use case

data.title: Poison messages block partitions
data.text: A message that crashes its consumer on every redelivery will, in a partition-committed-offset design, halt everything behind it. Every consumer needs a max-retry → DLQ path, and ops needs replay tooling for DLQ entries — otherwise one malformed payload becomes a multi-hour outage.

rows: Position of a message in the partition
Where a consumer group is reading

items: Rebalance storms: rolling deploys triggering partition churn — static group membership/cooperative rebalances limit the disruption
Producer ack lost after successful append — idempotent producer (sequence numbers per producer-partition) prevents duplicate appends
Follower lag beyond ISR — leader rejects writes (availability vs durability dial); alert before it happens
Consumer processes but crashes pre-commit — at-least-once delivers again; idempotency keys absorb it
Clock skew and timestamp semantics — event time vs broker time; downstream windows must use event time
Hot partition: one viral key gets 100% of traffic — salting or key redesign; partitions don't auto-fix skew

items.question: Kafka log vs SQS queue — how do you choose?
items.answer: Need replay, multiple independent consumer groups, or stream processing? Log. Need simple task distribution, per-message deletion, priority/delay? Queue. Many stacks end up with both, per workload.

items.question: How is consumer lag measured and governed?
items.answer: Lag = latest committed offset − group offset, per partition. Alert on lag growth rate and absolute values vs processing SLA; scale consumers up to partition count (no further parallelism possible beyond partitions).

items.question: Can you get true exactly-once?
items.answer: Only as end-to-end semantics: idempotent producers + transactional broker writes + idempotent consumers (dedupe store). Remove any link and you have at-least-once. Design for idempotency; treat 'exactly-once' as 'effectively-once by dedupe'.

items.question: What does a DLQ pipeline look like?
items.answer: Max retries → original message + error metadata → DLQ topic; dashboards and alerts on DLQ depth; ops tooling to inspect, fix, and replay to the source topic with the original key preserved.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Partition = ordering + parallelism unit; scale by partitioning on the right key
At-least-once + idempotent consumers is the realistic contract
Consumer lag is the health metric; DLQ + replay are mandatory ops paths
Log (Kafka) vs broker (SQS) shapes: replay/multi-consumer vs simple task semantics
data.takeaway: A queue system is a contract about failure: define your ordering scope, assume redelivery, and give poison messages somewhere to go but your pipeline.
